We begin our course at the atomic level. We will discuss how atoms are made up of charged and uncharged subatomic particles, and how these atoms can assemble into the molecules that make up your body.

slides.title: Part 1. Elements and compounds
slides.body:
Part 1. Elements and compounds

Matter
any substance that occupies space and has mass
what is not matter? light, heat, gravity, etc.
pure substances: elements, compounds (2+ elements) forming single substance
v.s., mixtures: combinations of substances

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024

Matter. Credit: Arman Cagle, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes:
Your body is made up of matter. Matter is any substance that occupies space and has mass. What is not classified as matter? Examples include light, heat, and gravity.

Matter usually comes in three main states: solid, liquid, or gas. 

In the next unit, we will discuss mixtures of matter. These are mixtures of substances, each of which retains its own chemical identity (e.g., solutions of salts or sugars dissolved in body fluids). However, in this unit, we’ll stick to a discussion of pure substances. Pure substances include elements (such as oxygen, O, or hydrogen, H), as well as compounds (combinations of two or more elements bonded together, such as carbon dioxide, CO2, or water, H20). Note that even though compounds are a combination of elements, they are themselves a single substance (e.g., the water), and are therefore not a mixture.

slides.title: Part 1. Elements and compounds
slides.body:
Part 1. Elements and compounds

Elements
matter of one type; cannot be created or broken down by ordinary chemical means

Elements of the Human Body. The main elements that compose the human body are shown from most abundant to least abundant.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
So, to restate, elements include matter of only one type. 

Elements cannot be created or broken down by ordinary chemical means. 

Examples of elements include oxygen (O), carbon (C), hydrogen (H), and nitrogen (N), the four most common elements found within your body.

Your body is made up of elements, but it cannot synthesize them—elements must be obtained from your external environment via food, drink, air, etc.

slides.title: Part 1. Elements and compounds
slides.body:
Part 1. Elements and compounds

Atoms
single units of an element
e.g., one atom of oxygen
Molecules
two or more atoms covalently bonded together (atoms share electrons).
can be of the same element type; e.g., oxygen (O2)
can be of different element types; e.g., carbon dioxide (CO2)
Compounds
a substance composed of two or more different elements joined by chemical bonds (does not need to be covalent bond)
e.g., carbon dioxide (CO2)
note that CO2 and is a molecule and a compound, while O2 is only a molecule

Adapted from Figure 5. b) An atom of the element O.

Figure 5. b) A molecule of O2.

Figure 5. c) CO2 is both a molecule and a compound.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The smallest units of elements are called atoms. Think of them as a single unit of an element. An example of an atom would be one oxygen (O).

Atoms can be assembled into molecules via covalent bonds (whereby the atoms share electrons—we’ll cover this topic in more detail soon). If you put two oxygen atoms together, you get oxygen (O2), a component of the air that we breathe. This can be called dioxygen, but is commonly referred to as just oxygen. Note that O2 is not a compound because both atoms are of the same type of element (oxygen)! Molecules can also comprise atoms of two or more types of elements. In this latter case, the molecule is also called a compound.

A compound is therefore a molecule made up of at least two different types of elements joined by a chemical bond. I provided examples of some of these earlier: carbon dioxide (CO2) and water (H20). Carbon dioxide contains atoms of both carbon and oxygen. Water contains atoms of both oxygen and hydrogen.

Water (H20).

Fischer projection of D-glucose. Credit: Hmxhmx at English Wikipedia, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

slides.notes:
All compounds can be categorized by the nature of their constituent elements. An inorganic compound is a substance that does not contain both carbon and hydrogen. An example of this would be water (H20).

An organic compound is a substance that contains carbon-hydrogen bonds. An example would be glucose (C6H12O6). It is a three-dimensional compound, but the image here shows a two-dimensional projection for simplicity.

Carbon atoms are the structural backbones of many large, complex organic molecules in your body
e.g., a triglyceride is a common type of fat stored in your body

A triglyceride from dairy butter. Credit: Smokefoot, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

A ball and stick model of a triglyceride fat. Credit: Kdv2754, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

slides.notes:
Carbon atoms can bind to other carbon atoms, and atoms of many other elements, allowing the building of large, complex organic molecules for use in your body. 

For example, these two images show a triglyceride, a type of fat that is used for energy storage in your body. The image on the left is a ball and stick model where the carbons are shown in grey and form the backbone of the three long chains. Because there are so many carbons (and associated hydrogens) in organic molecules, they are often left out in linear drawings of compounds, and are simply assumed to be in the regions where two lines meet, such as in the diagram on the right.

When you break covalent bonds, you can use that energy to form new bonds
e.g., when breaking down triglyceride

ATP molecules store energy from metabolism of food molecules, and transfer that energy to other bodily processes when ATP is split to ADP and a phosphate group. Credit: Lisawerner9, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
When you break covalent bonds (the bonds formed from the sharing of electrons), you can transfer that energy to the formation of new bonds.

This is true when you break down the triglycerides from the last slide, or when you cleave a phosphate group from a molecule of adenosine triphosphate (ATP), to create adenosine diphosphate (ADP). ATP is an essential energy transfer molecule in your body.

slides.title: Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles
slides.body:
Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles

All atoms, regardless of the element, are made up of a combination of the same three subatomic particles:
protons
a heavy subatomic particle having a positive charge and found in the atom’s nucleus
neutrons
a heavy subatomic particle having no electrical charge and found in the atom’s nucleus
electrons
a subatomic particle having a negative charge and nearly no mass; found orbiting the atom’s nucleus

Subatomic particles of an atom. Credit: Svdmolen/Jeanot (converted by King of Hearts), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Subatomic Attitudes. Credit: Christinelmiller, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Recall that an atom is the smallest quantity of an element that retains the unique properties of that element – a single unit.

All atoms, regardless of the element, are made up of a combination of the same three subatomic particles:

Protons: A heavy subatomic particle having a positive charge and found in the atom’s nucleus.

Neutrons: A heavy subatomic particle having no electrical charge and found in the atom’s nucleus.

Electrons: A subatomic particle having a negative charge and nearly no mass; found orbiting the atom’s nucleus.

The number of heavy protons and neutrons gives mass to the atom.

The number of protons in the nucleus of the atom determine the element.

slides.title: Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles
slides.body:
Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles

E.g., Helium (He) has two protons, two neutrons, and two electrons
electrons sometimes drawn in orbit, but are actually found within an electron cloud
electrons and protons attracted to one another, stabilizing atom
atoms with equal number of protons and electrons have a balanced charge

Figure 2. Two Models of Atomic Structure. (a) In the planetary model, the electrons of helium are shown in fixed orbits, depicted as rings, at a precise distance from the nucleus, somewhat like planets orbiting the sun. (b) In the electron cloud model, the electrons of helium are shown in the variety of locations they would have at different distances from the nucleus over time.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
For instance, helium (He), is composed of two protons, two neutrons, and two electrons.

In the planetary model (or Bohr model), helium’s two electrons are shown circling the nucleus in a fixed orbit depicted as a ring (Figure 2a). Although this model is helpful in visualizing atomic structure, in reality, electrons do not travel in fixed orbits, but whiz around the nucleus erratically in a so-called electron cloud (Figure 2b).

The positively charged protons attract the negatively charged electrons. This mutual attraction gives the atom structural stability. 

The number of protons and electrons within a neutral atom are equal, thus, the atom’s overall charge is balanced.

slides.title: Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles
slides.body:
Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles

Because helium has two protons, it has an atomic number of 2.

A simplified periodic table of elements. Credit: User:Double sharp, based on File:Simple Periodic Table Chart-en.svg by User:Offnfopt, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Because helium has two protons, it has an atomic number of 2. No other elements have atoms containing 2 protons. If an atom had only 1 proton, it would be hydrogen. If it had 6 protons, it would be carbon. Thus, the number of protons in the nucleus of the atom identifies the element. This is a simplified periodic table of element that only shows elements’ atomic numbers and chemical symbols. Full periodic tables also include other information, such as an element’s mass.

slides.title: Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles
slides.body:
Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles

An element’s mass number is the sum of the protons and neutrons
e.g., 2 neutrons + 2 protons = 4 (the mass number for helium)

Helium. Credit: Albedo-ukr, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

Figure 2. Two Models of Atomic Structure. (a) In the planetary model, the electrons of helium are shown in fixed orbits, depicted as rings, at a precise distance from the nucleus, somewhat like planets orbiting the sun. (b) In the electron cloud model, the electrons of helium are shown in the variety of locations they would have at different distances from the nucleus over time.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In their most common form, many elements contain the same number of neutrons as protons.

Because the most common form of helium has 2 protons and 2 neutrons, its mass number is 4 (the sum of these two large subatomic particles—the mass of the tiny electrons is negligible, so they do not factor into the calculation).

Thus, the atomic number of helium is 2 and the mass number is 4.

slides.title: Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles
slides.body:
Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles

Formation & breakage of substances due to electrons in reactions:
electrons tend to stay within electron shells
1st electron shell holds up to two electrons, 2nd up to eight, 3rd up to 18
all electron shells, apart from the first shell, are considered “complete” with eight electrons
a complete valence shell, makes an atom non-reactive (e.g., neon)
carbon is reactive as only 4 of 8 electrons present in valence shell – makes it reactive and the basis of most biological molecules

Electron Shells. Electrons orbit the atomic nucleus at distinct levels of energy called electron shells. (a) With one electron, hydrogen only half-fills its electron shell. Helium also has a single shell, but its two electrons completely fill it. (b) The electrons of carbon completely fill its first electron shell, but only half-fills its second. (c) Neon, an element that does not occur in the body, has 10 electrons, filling both of its electron shells.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In the human body, atoms do not exist as independent entities. Rather, they are constantly interacting to form complex substances, or to break complex substances down. To fully understand anatomy and physiology you must grasp how atoms participate in such reactions. The key is understanding the behavior of electrons.

Although electrons do not follow rigid orbits a set distance away from the atom’s nucleus, they do tend to stay within certain regions of space called electron shells. An electron shell is a layer of electrons that encircle the nucleus at a distinct energy level.

The atoms of the elements found in the human body have from one to five electron shells, but we’ll stick to smaller elements with fewer shells in this course. The first electron shell holds up to two electrons. The second holds up to eight. The third holds up to 18. 

Hydrogen and helium have just one and two electrons, respectively. They are the only elements with one electron shell.

All electron shells, apart from the first shell, are considered “complete” with eight electrons. When the outer-most shell, called the valence shell is complete, that atom is non-reactive—its electrons are unlikely to be pulled away by other atoms, or to pull another atom’s electrons to itself.

In this example, neon has 10 electrons, so two fill its first shell, and the remaining eight completely fill its second shell—thus making neon non-reactive.

Carbon, on the other hand, possesses solely six electrons; two fill its first shell, and the second shell is only half-filled with the remaining four. This half-filled shell makes carbon reactive and an ideal element for forming bonds with other elements, which can lead to the construction of complex structures for your body, as well as in all living things. Hence, the term “carbon-based life”.

slides.title: Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles
slides.body:
Part 1. Atoms and subatomic particles

Hydrogen has a smaller valence shell that is complete with two electrons
Hydrogen interacts with elements such as carbon and oxygen to share electrons to fill each other’s valence shells
this is the basis for covalent bonds (discussed soon)

Water. Credit: Lm4p3y6, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Electron Shells. Electrons orbit the atomic nucleus at distinct levels of energy called electron shells. (a) With one electron, hydrogen only half-fills its electron shell. Helium also has a single shell, but its two electrons completely fill it. (b) The electrons of carbon completely fill its first electron shell, but only half-fills its second.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Recall that organic compounds contain carbon-hydrogen bonds. The reason why these are so common is that hydrogen tends to share electrons with carbon. Recall that hydrogen has only one electron in its valence shell, the first electron shell, which can hold two electrons in total. Thus, its valence shell is incomplete. The single electron is likely to be drawn into relationships with the atoms of other elements, like carbon, so that it can share one of the other element’s electrons and make its valence shell complete with that extra electron.

Likewise, oxygen has six electrons in its outer shell. It can interact with two hydrogen ions to form water. By doing so, the oxygen shares each of the two extra electrons to bring its valence shell to a complete set of eight, while each of the two hydrogens shares one of the oxygen molecule’s electrons to complete its smaller valence shell at two electrons.

This sharing of electrons is the basis of covalent bonds. But that is just one type of bond—a subject to which we turn next.

slides.title: Part 2. Ions and ionic bonds
slides.body:
Part 2. Ions and ionic bonds

Ions
atoms that donate or accept electrons in order to have a full valence shell
donating electrons generates an ion with a positive charge: a cation
e.g.,. sodium to sodium cation
accepting electrons leads to an ion with a negative charge: an anion
e.g., fluorine to fluoride anion

An atomic joke. Credit: Christinelmiller, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Formation of ionic Sodium Fluoride. Credit: Wdcf, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In the previous examples, we discussed atoms sharing electrons to form covalent bonds, and we’ll get back to that shortly. We’re instead going to begin this section with a discussion of ions and ionic bonds. 

Recall that an atom normally has the same number of protons and electrons, and thus the positive and negative charges cancel out, leaving the atom electrically neutral. This is not always the case, however. Atoms sometimes participate in chemical reactions where one or more electrons are donated by an atom, leaving it with a positive charge, or where an atom accepts one or more electrons, leading to it acquiring a negative charge. Hence the joke in the top figure—losing an electron makes an atom positive.

Some atoms accept electrons to fill their valence shell to eight electrons. Other atoms donate electrons to empty a valence shell completely, meaning that the next lowest (complete) electron shell becomes the new (outermost) valence shell. 

An atom that has an electrical charge—whether positive or negative—is an ion.

In the bottom example, sodium donates the single electron in its third electron shell, causing its second electron shell to become a complete valence shell. Because the sodium has become a positive sodium ion, a cation, we write its chemical symbol as Na+. The fluorine accepts the electron, causing its valence shell to also become full. It becomes negative; this anion is now called fluoride, and is written as F-.

Atoms that have more than one electron to donate or accept will end up with stronger positive or negative charges. For example, calcium donates two electrons and so is written as Ca2+.

slides.title: Part 2. Ions and ionic bonds
slides.body:
Part 2. Ions and ionic bonds

Ionic bonds
cations and anions are attracted to one another
table salt (the ionic compound NaCl) is the result of ionic bonding between Na+ and Cl- ions
water breaks up ionically bonded substances to individual ions – their main form in your body
marketed as electrolytes in sports drinks

Ionic Bonding. (a) Sodium readily donates the solitary electron in its valence shell to chlorine, which needs only one electron to have a full valence shell. (b) The opposite electrical charges of the resulting sodium cation and chloride anion result in the formation of a bond of attraction called an ionic bond. (c) The attraction of many sodium and chloride ions results in the formation of large groupings called crystals.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The opposite charges of cations and anions exert a moderately strong mutual attraction that keeps the atoms in close proximity forming an ionic bond. For example, table salt is the result of ionic bonding between sodium and chloride. Sodium donates an electron, becoming the cation Na+, while chloride accepts that electron, becoming the anion Cl-. The cations and anions are attracted to each other, forming the compound NaCl (recall that a compound is a substance composed of two or more different elements joined by chemical bonds).

Water is an essential component of life because it is able to break the ionic bonds in salts (like table salt) to free the ions. Thus, in biological fluids, the table salt that you ingest typically exists as separate sodium and chloride ions. These dissolved ions produce electrical charges within the body, and later in the course we will discuss how these electrical charges are integral in processes such as muscle contraction and action potential signaling through neurons. We will also discuss how you can track the electrical currents caused by these ions via techniques such as an electrocardiogram for the heart or an electroencephalogram, for the brain.

The electrical activity that derives from the interactions of the charged ions is why they are also called electrolytes—those components that sport drink companies market as needing to be replaced after exercising and losing ions via sweat.

slides.title: Part 2. Covalent bonds
slides.body:
Part 2. Covalent bonds

Covalent Bonds
electrons in the outermost valence shell are shared to fill the valence shells of both atoms
strong; not broken by water
nonpolar covalent bonds: balanced, equal sharing of electrons

Covalent bonding. a) A single covalent bond: hydrogen gas (H-H). Two atoms of hydrogen each share their solitary election in a single covalent bond. b) A double covalent bond: oxygen gas (O=O). An atom of oxygen has its electrons in its valence shell: thus, two more would make it stable. Two atoms of oxygen achieve stability by sharing two pairs of electrons in a double covalent bond. c) Two double covalent bonds: carbon dioxide (O=C=O). An atom of carbon has four electrons in its valence shell; thus, four more would make it stable. An atom of carbon and two atoms of oxygen achieve stability by sharing two electron pairs each, in two double covalent bonds.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Okay, so now that we’ve covered ionic bonds, let us return to covalent bonds.

Unlike ionic bonds formed by the attraction between a cation’s positive charge and an anion’s negative charge, molecules formed by a covalent bond share electrons in a mutually stabilizing relationship. 

Covalent bonds are strong. Because of the close sharing of electrons, most covalent bonds are not broken apart in water.

The figure on the right shows several common types of covalent bonds. Covalently bonded atoms typically share just one or two electron pairs, though larger sharings are possible. Single covalent bonds are shown in (a) for hydrogen gas, H2, and in (b) for oxygen gas, O2; (c) shows a double bond, where carbon shares all of its four electrons in its valence shell—two with one atom of oxygen, and the other two with a second atom of oxygen—the resulting compound is carbon dioxide, or CO2.

Note that the bonds shown on this page are all nonpolar covalent bonds because they are balanced, with an equal sharing of electrons between atoms.

slides.title: Part 2. Covalent bonds
slides.body:
Part 2. Covalent bonds

Covalent Bonds
polar covalent bonds: unbalanced, unequal sharing of electrons
results in regions of a molecule having opposite partial charges = a dipole

A water molecule. Credit: Ingvald Straume, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

Polar Covalent Bonds in a Water Molecule.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Polar covalent bonds differ from nonpolar covalent bonds in that atoms share electrons unequally, resulting in regions of a molecule having opposite charges

The most familiar example of a polar molecule is water (shown in the figure). The molecule has three parts: one atom of oxygen, the nucleus of which contains eight protons, and two hydrogen atoms, whose nuclei each contain only one proton. Because every proton exerts an identical positive charge, a nucleus that contains eight protons exerts a charge eight times greater than a nucleus that contains one proton. This means that the negatively charged electrons present in the water molecule are more strongly attracted to the oxygen nucleus than to the hydrogen nuclei. Each hydrogen atom’s single negative electron therefore migrates toward the oxygen atom, making the oxygen end of their bond slightly more negative than the hydrogen end of their bond.

These slight charges are also referred to as “partial charges” because the strength of the charge is less than one full electron, as would occur in an ionic bond.  Regions of weak polarity are indicated in diagrams with the Greek letter delta (∂) and a plus (+) or minus (–) sign. The opposing electrical charges on the molecule pull that mass in such a way that it creates a shape somewhat like a triangular tent, creating a dipole, a molecule with a negatively charged portion separated from a positively charged portion.

slides.title: Part 2. Hydrogen bonds
slides.body:
Part 2. Hydrogen bonds

Hydrogen bond
weakly positive hydrogen atom (∂+ from being part of a covalent bond) binds to an electronegative atom (∂-) from another molecule

Hydrogen Bonds between Water Molecules. Notice that the bonds occur between the slightly (or weakly) positive charge on the hydrogen atoms and the slightly (or weakly) negative charge on the oxygen atoms. Hydrogen bonds are relatively weak, and therefore are indicated with a dotted (rather than a solid) line.

A water strider stands on the water because of its light weight and the surface tension of the water. Credit: NPS Photo, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
A hydrogen bond is formed when a weakly positive hydrogen atom already bonded to one electronegative atom (for example, the oxygen in the water molecule) is attracted to another electronegative atom from another molecule. 

Hydrogen bonds thus always include a hydrogen atom that is already part of a polar molecule.

A common example of a hydrogen bond is between molecules of water (as shown in the figure). Hydrogen bonding occurs because the slightly negative oxygen atom in one water molecule is attracted to the slightly positive hydrogen atoms of two other water molecules. This creates surface tension, and is the reason why some insects can walk on water. In the second A&P course in this series, we will discuss how our lungs need to secrete a substance called surfactant, which breaks up the surface tension of water on the surface of your lungs to prevent them from collapsing due to the attraction of water molecules on one surface to water molecules on another surface.

slides.title: Part 2. Dipole Interactions
slides.body:
Part 2. Dipole Interactions

Dipole-Ion bonds
the partial charges on water molecules pull NaCl apart (for the table salt to dissolve in water)
many water molecules combine, so weaker dipole charges prevail over ionic bond
the weakly positive portion of water interacts with the Cl- anion
the weakly negative portion of water interacts with the Na+ cation
Dipole charges repel nonpolar covalent bonds
the partial charges on water repel nonpolar molecules like fats, lipids and oils

Dissociation of Sodium Chloride in Water. Credit: OpenStax College, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Water molecules also strongly attract other types of charged molecules as well as ions. This explains why sodium chloride or “table salt,” for example, dissolves so readily in water. In this case dipole–ion bonds form between the water and the electrically-charged ions, allowing water molecules to pull the Na+ cations and Cl– anions away from each other. 

On the other hand, water molecules repel molecules with nonpolar covalent bonds, like fats, lipids, and oils. You can demonstrate this with a simple kitchen experiment: pour a teaspoon of vegetable oil, a compound formed by nonpolar covalent bonds, into a glass of water. Instead of dissolving in the water, the oil forms a distinct bead because the polar water molecules repel the nonpolar oil.

slides.title: Part 2. Dipole Interactions
slides.body:
Part 2. Dipole Interactions

Physical properties of water
hydrogen bonds give water special properties:
density – for a typical substance, the solid state is denser than the liquid state, but ice is less dense than water
boiling point – based on chemical trends indicate that water should have a boiling point of -90⁰C; however, the actual boiling point of water is 100⁰C
specific heat capacity – water requires an unusually high amount of energy be added to increase its temperature (and releases an unusually high amount of energy when cooled)

Hydrogen Bonds between Water Molecules. Notice that the bonds occur between the slightly (or weakly) positive charge on the hydrogen atoms and the slightly (or weakly) negative charge on the oxygen atoms. Hydrogen bonds are relatively weak, and therefore are indicated with a dotted (rather than a solid) line.
slides.notes: The formation of hydrogen bonds in water allows water to have different physical properties than other liquids. One is density; for a typical substance, the solid state is denser than the liquid state. However, this is not the case for water, as ice (solid state) is actually less dense than water (liquid state). The formation of hydrogen bonds in water also affects its boiling point. Scientific predictions based on chemical trends indicate that water should have a boiling point of -90⁰C. However, the actual boiling point of water is 100⁰C. In a similar manner, hydrogen bonding also affects the specific heat capacity of water, so that water requires an unusually high amount of energy be added to increase its temperature (and releases an unusually high amount of energy when cooled).
